newsitem.title: USA: Miami Heat sue to block arena bond vote.
newsitem.headline: Miami Heat sue to block arena bond vote.

text.p: The Miami Heat filed suit Wednesday seeking to block a Dade County referendum on proposed bond financing for a new basketball arena.

"The petition that formed the basis for this referendum is misleading, vague and clearly violates Dade County's Charter and Code, as well as state election laws," Heat General Counsel Eric Woolworth said in a prepared statement.

Dade County has agreed to issue $165 million of revenue bonds to build the arena on public park land adjacent to Port of Miami. It is part of a waterfront development program that includes construction of new cruise ship terminals, parking and retail space.
Debt service was to be paid with arena revenues, a sales tax rebate and revenues from an existing hotel bed tax.
A local attorney, Dan Paul, opposed both the use of tax money and public land. He collected enough voter signatures to force a Nov 5 referendum on the financing plan.
Woolworth said the petitions were improper because they addressed several different issues, and did not make clear all the possible consequences of rejecting the plan.
"The present language only serves to confuse voters on the issues of a new arena, port project and future waterfront development," Woolworth said.
Paul, who was not named as a respondent, said his political action committee, Stop The New Arena Committee, would seek to intervene in the lawsuit.
"We will defend the public's right to vote to the hilt. This is the final act of arrogance on the part of the Heat to try to deny the public the right to vote," Paul said.
Woolworth said the Heat objected to the ballot language, but not to the referendum process.

"We strongly support the right of Dade County voters to vote on matters initiated by petition, so long as they are voting on a valid proposal that is misleading. Unfortunately that is not he case here," Woolworth said.
Dade County Elections Supervisor David Leahy, who was named as a respondent in the lawsuit, said his staff was already in the process of getting the ballots printed.
"If the court takes it off, we simply will not count the votes. If there's time, we can stamp something across it," Leahy said.
Dade County attorneys were not immediately available for comment.
